title: My Portfolio
text: Welcome to my Engineering Portfolio! I am a rising Junior Engineering major at Harvey Mudd College interested in mechanical and electrical engineering. I’m currently doing a Manufacturing Engineering internship for General Motors at their Autonomous Robotic Center. I am also a Machine Shop Proctor and work on the mechanical subteam for the FSAE team.

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
AUV Robot





Climate change and ocean health monitoring require scalable, low-cost solutions for collecting environmental data. This project was motivated by the need to develop an autonomous system capable of measuring key ocean parameters at varying depths without human intervention. The goal was to design a robot that could reliably collect pressure, temperature, and UV data in real marine environments and contribute meaningful data for climate research.

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
Contributions

Led electrical system design, implementing 3 analog circuits with voltage-to-voltage, current-to-voltage, and resistance-to-voltage interfaces
Engineered UV, pressure, and temperature sensor systems using a unity-gain buffer and inverting gain amplifier to optimize data resolution and prevent clipping on the Teensy 4.0
Developed calibration protocols accounting for noise, sensor non-linearity, and degradation for accurate underwater measurements
Designed and fabricated a mechanically stable system maintaining neutral buoyancy in saltwater while minimizing axial tilt
Developed a C++ algorithm for dynamic depth control, enabling autonomous waypoint navigation at various depths
Created MATLAB scripts to process and visualize temperature and UV intensity as a function of depth for climate monitoring analysis

title: My Portfolio
text:
GENERAL MOTORS — Manufacturing Engineering Intern : Autonomous Robotics Center
This past summer, I interned at General Motors’ Autonomous Robotics Center in Burton, Michigan as a Manufacturing Engineering Intern. I was embedded directly on the floor of a live processing plant, supporting the launch and integration of an Automated Storage and Retrieval System (ASRS) — a large-scale automation initiative aimed at transforming how materials are stored, retrieved, and delivered across production departments.
My role placed me at the intersection of engineering and operations, where I worked alongside cross-functional teams to redesign material-handling workflows, analyze production data, and develop workstation concepts that would support the seamless transition to a more automated environment.
I also had the privilege of developing and earning a Green Belt in Design for Six Sigma (DFSS) — a certification that has fundamentally shaped how I approach engineering problems. DFSS trained me to minimize variation and bias in process design, allowing me to build fine-tuned solutions that are statistically validated.

DASION — Software Engineer & ML Intern
This past summer, I interned at Dasion as a Software Engineer and Machine Learning Intern based in Claremont, California. Dasion is a data-driven company focused on leveraging machine learning to support medical and behavioral research. My role placed me at the intersection of software engineering and applied machine learning, where I worked on developing tools to support emotion recognition in children using medical imaging data.
Working on a project with real clinical implications pushed me to think carefully about model selection, data quality, and the downstream impact of engineering decisions. Every preprocessing step, every architecture choice, and every evaluation metric carried weight — because the end users were researchers and practitioners working with vulnerable populations.
One of the most exciting aspects of this internship was building an emotion-based music recommender using the Spotify API — a creative application that connected the emotional state detected by our models to curated playlists, demonstrating the real-world potential of the system beyond clinical settings.

HARVEY MUDD COLLEGE — Machine Shop Proctor
The Harvey Mudd Machine Shop serves as a creative space for the 7 Claremont Colleges, welcoming people from all different backgrounds in machining to work on personal projects, class projects, and team projects — allowing for the full spectrum of the creative space to come to life. The shop features both a wooden shop and a metal shop, each equipped with a variety of tools that support everything from early-stage prototyping to precision manufacturing.
As a Machine Shop Proctor, my role is to guide new and existing users on safe practices while assisting with project development for classes. This means being present on the floor, understanding what each person is trying to build, and helping them navigate the right tools, techniques, and processes to get there — safely and effectively.
Beyond day-to-day guidance, I participate in weekly trainings that continuously build my knowledge of machining, tooling, and manufacturing processes. These sessions have deepened my understanding of the machines I work with and made me a more effective resource for the students and makers who rely on the shop.
I also play a direct role in supporting engineering courses at Harvey Mudd, including Introduction to Engineering Design and Manufacturing and Mechanical Design, where I guide students through reading and following process routers and technical drawings to manufacture components to specification — skills that form the foundation of any engineering career.

title: Flexible Measuring Laser
text:
Flexible Measuring Laser





The users using the scanning electron microscope (SEM) need to manually estimate the height of their mounted samples and enter that height electronically into the microscope settings before they place it in the microscope. This process requires the user to visually compare the sample against a ruler, which is likely inconsistent for the most part, causing inaccurate measurements. Inaccurate height inputs can possibly lead to collisions when inside the microscope chamber, causing damage to the sensitive detectors or possibly limiting its performance. The client wants a height measurement solution that allows trained users to quickly, safely, and accurately determine the maximum sample height for any standard SEM sample holder. The solution must be able to accommodate all existing holder bases, which have at most a 10 cm radius and sample diameters of 26 mm, while providing readouts with a tolerance of 0.5 mm without contacting the surface of the sample [1]. Additionally, it is very important that nothing touches the top of the sample during the measuring process [2]. The top of the sample is covered in a conductive coating that is on the scale of nanometers thick [2]. Therefore, anything that brushes along the top of the sample could cause damage to the coating and sample itself [1,2]. The solution should be simple to use, highly durable, easily cleaned, minimized the need for calibration while allowing trained non-specialist users to get accurate measurements in under two minutes. The measurement process must be quick in order to make it more convenient for the user because this step should be a relatively simple step in the entire process of using the electron microscope.

title: Flexible Measuring Laser
text:
Contributions

Designed a precision rack and pinion Z-axis measurement system achieving less than 1mm accuracy for SEM sample preparation
Integrated a laser and photosensor along with a slew bearing for radial motion to detect the tallest point on samples of variable height
Optimized durability through full material and fatigue analysis, selecting powder nylon (SLS nylon) for superior wear resistance, strength, and dimensional stability under high cycle use
Delivered a scalable, easily replicable design that improves SEM workflow safety and prevents $1000+ in potential equipment damage from improper sample height

title: Machinist’s Hammer
text:
Hammer Front





Precision machining is a fundamental skill in mechanical engineering, requiring the ability to read and interpret technical drawings and manufacture components to tight tolerances. This project was motivated by the need to develop hands-on machining skills using industry-standard equipment and processes. The goal was to manufacture a fully functional machinist hammer from raw materials including clear oak, steel, and nylon, adhering to detailed engineering drawings and dimensional tolerances. Furthermore this project contributes to the Harvey Mudd College tradition of student-made hammers.

title: Submersible Robot with Kp Control
text:
Submersible Robot





Underwater remotely operated vehicles provide a cost-effective solution for retrieving environmental data in aquatic settings. This project was motivated by the need to design and deploy a functional ROV capable of measuring temperature and pressure signals in lake environments. The goal was to develop a system that could reliably collect sensor data and process output voltages for analysis in LabVIEW.
